column1: Sims’s original work used log levels of U.S. nominal GNP and money (both M1 and the monetary base). He found evidence that money Granger-caused GNP. That is, the past behavior of money helped to predict future GNP. However, using the index of industrial production to measure real output, Sims (1980) found that the fraction of output variation explained by money was greatly reduced when a nominal interest rate was added to the equation (so that z consists of the log price level and an interest rate). Thus, the conclusion seemed sensitive to the specification of z. Eichenbaum and Singleton (1987) found that money appeared to be less important if the regressions were specified in log first di¤erence form rather than in log levels with a time trend. Stock and Watson (1989) provided a systematic treatment of the trend specification in testing whether money Granger-causes real output. They concluded that money does help to predict future output (they actually used industrial production) even when prices and an interest rate are included.
